{{Short description|Category theory generalization of fumction factorization}}
In [[mathematics]], it can be shown that every [[function (mathematics)|function]] can be written as the composite of a [[surjective]] function followed by an [[injective]] function. '''Factorization systems''' are a generalization of this situation in [[category theory]].

==Definition==

A '''factorization system''' (''E'', ''M'') for a [[category (category theory)|category]] '''C''' consists of two classes of [[morphisms]] ''E'' and ''M'' of '''C''' such that:
#''E'' and ''M'' both contain all [[isomorphisms]] of '''C''' and are closed under composition.
#Every morphism ''f'' of '''C''' can be factored as <math>f=m\circ e</math> for some morphisms <math>e\in E</math> and <math>m\in M</math>.
#The factorization is ''functorial'': if <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> are two morphisms such that <math>vme=m'e'u</math> for some morphisms <math>e, e'\in E</math> and <math>m, m'\in M</math>, then there exists a unique morphism <math>w</math> making the following diagram [[commutative diagram|commute]]:
[[Image:Factorization_system_functoriality.png|center]]


''Remark:'' <math>(u,v)</math> is a morphism from <math>me</math> to <math>m'e'</math> in the [[Comma_category#Arrow_category|arrow category]].

== Orthogonality ==

Two morphisms <math>e</math> and <math>m</math> are said to be ''orthogonal'', denoted <math>e\downarrow m</math>, if for every pair of morphisms <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> such that <math>ve=mu</math> there is a unique morphism <math>w</math> such that the diagram

[[Image:Factorization_system_orthogonality.png|center]]

commutes. This notion can be extended to define the orthogonals of sets of morphisms by

:<math>H^\uparrow=\{e\quad|\quad\forall h\in H, e\downarrow h\}</math> and <math>H^\downarrow=\{m\quad|\quad\forall h\in H, h\downarrow m\}.</math>

Since in a factorization system <math>E\cap M</math> contains all the isomorphisms, the condition (3) of the definition is equivalent to
:(3') <math>E\subseteq M^\uparrow</math> and <math>M\subseteq E^\downarrow.</math>


''Proof:'' In the previous diagram (3), take <math> m:= id ,\  e' := id </math> (identity on the appropriate object) and <math> m' := m </math>.

== Equivalent definition ==
The pair <math>(E,M)</math> of classes of morphisms of '''C''' is a factorization system if and only if it satisfies the following conditions:

#Every morphism ''f'' of '''C''' can be factored as <math>f=m\circ e</math> with <math>e\in E</math> and <math>m\in M.</math>
#<math>E=M^\uparrow</math> and <math>M=E^\downarrow.</math>

== Weak factorization systems ==
Suppose ''e'' and ''m'' are two morphisms in a category '''C'''. Then ''e'' has the ''[[right lifting property|left lifting property]]'' with respect to ''m'' (respectively ''m'' has the ''[[right lifting property]]'' with respect to ''e'') when for every pair of morphisms ''u'' and ''v'' such that ''ve''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''mu'' there is a morphism ''w'' such that the following diagram commutes. The difference with orthogonality is that ''w'' is not necessarily unique.

[[Image:Factorization_system_orthogonality.png|center]]

A '''weak factorization system''' (''E'', ''M'') for a category '''C''' consists of two classes of morphisms ''E'' and ''M'' of '''C''' such that:<ref>{{harvtxt|Riehl|2014|loc=§11.2}}</ref>
#The class ''E'' is exactly the class of morphisms having the left lifting property with respect to each morphism in ''M''.
#The class ''M'' is exactly the class of morphisms having the right lifting property with respect to each morphism in ''E''.
#Every morphism ''f'' of '''C''' can be factored as <math>f=m\circ e</math> for some morphisms <math>e\in E</math> and <math>m\in M</math>.
This notion leads to a succinct definition of [[model category|model categories]]: a model category is a pair consisting of a category '''C''' and classes of (so-called) [[weak equivalence (homotopy theory)|weak equivalence]]s ''W'', fibrations ''F'' and cofibrations ''C'' so that

* '''C'''  has all [[limit (category theory)|limit]]s and colimits,

* <math>(C \cap W, F)</math> is a weak factorization system,

* <math>(C, F \cap W)</math> is a weak factorization system, and

* <math>W</math> satisfies the two-out-of-three property: if <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are composable morphisms and two of <math>f,g,g\circ f</math> are in <math>W</math>, then so is the third.<ref>{{harvtxt|Riehl|2014|loc=§11.3}}</ref>

A model category is a complete and cocomplete category equipped with a model structure. A map is called a trivial fibration if it belongs to <math>F\cap W,</math> and it is called a trivial [[cofibration]] if it belongs to <math>C\cap W.</math> An object <math>X</math> is called fibrant if the morphism <math>X\rightarrow 1</math> to the [[Initial and terminal objects|terminal object]] is a fibration, and it is called cofibrant if the morphism <math>0\rightarrow X</math> from the initial object is a cofibration.<ref>Valery Isaev - On fibrant objects in model categories.</ref>
